metadata.shortDescription: Starting a tax overage business can be a lucrative venture if done correctly. Tax overages, also called tax lien surplus or excess proceeds, arise when a property is sold at a tax sale for more than the amount owed in taxes and fees. The original property owner may be entitled to claim those surplus funds, and your business can help locate, notify, and assist those owners in reclaiming their money for a fee. Using free AI tools can streamline much of the research, outreach, and marketing involved in launching this type of business. This step-by-step guide will walk you through the process of starting a tax overage business with the help of free AI, making the journey easier, smarter, and more efficient.

segments.text: For the best experience, please turn on subtitles while watching this video so
you can easily follow the AI resources and prompt texts shared throughout.
If you'd like to copy the names of the AI tools and the wording of the prompts

lucrative venture if done correctly. Tax overages, also called tax lien surplus or excess proceeds,
arise when a property is sold at a tax sale for more than the amount owed in taxes and fees.
The original property owner may be entitled to claim those surplus funds, and your business can
help locate, notify, and assist those owners in reclaiming their money for a fee. Using
free AI tools can streamline much of the research, outreach, and marketing involved in launching this
type of business. This step-by-step guide will walk you through the process of starting a tax
overage business with the help of free AI, making the journey easier, smarter, and more efficient.
Step 1: Understand the Tax Overage Business Model and Legal Framework
Before diving in, you need a solid understanding of what tax overage is, how the surplus funds are
generated, and the legal process for claiming them in your target states or counties. Tax
laws and processes vary widely by location, so it’s essential to research the rules governing
tax overage claims in your chosen area. Use free AI research tools like ChatGPT or other
AI-powered search engines to help you summarize local tax codes, statutes, and procedures.
For example, you can prompt ChatGPT: “Explain how tax overage funds are
handled in [state/county]. What are the legal requirements to claim surplus tax sale funds?”
Step 2: Define Your Target Market and Service Offering
Decide if your business will focus on locating property owners with overage funds,
assisting them in filing claims, or both. Also, determine whether you’ll work with residential or
commercial properties or both. To help create a clear business plan, use an AI tool like ChatGPT
to draft your plan. Try a prompt such as: “Create a business plan outline for a tax overage recovery
service focusing on [state or county]. Include sections on market analysis, service offerings,
revenue model, and marketing strategy.” This will give you a structured roadmap to follow.
Step 3: Research and Gather Data on Tax Sales and Overage Funds
Your business depends on accurate data about tax sales and surplus funds. Many counties publish
auction results and surplus fund listings online. Use free web scraping and data extraction AI tools
such as Octoparse or ParseHub to automate data collection. These tools help you gather lists of
properties with overage funds, owner information, sale dates, and amounts. If you want to generate
custom queries or process large data files, tools like ChatGPT can assist in writing scripts or
parsing data. For example, prompt: “Help me write a Python script to extract owner names
and surplus amounts from a tax sale results PDF.” Step 4: Build a Client Outreach Strategy Using AI
Once you have your data, you need to reach out to potential clients—the property owners
eligible to claim overage funds. Use AI to craft personalized outreach messages, letters, and email
campaigns. ChatGPT is perfect for generating professional and persuasive communication.
You might prompt it with: “Write a formal letter to a property owner informing them about potential
surplus tax sale funds they can claim, including an introduction to my recovery service and a call
to action.” You can then adapt these messages for emails, phone scripts, or direct mail.
Step 5: Develop a Website and Online Presence with AI Assistance
In today’s digital world, having a professional website is critical.
Free AI website builders like Wix ADI or Bookmark can help you create a simple but
effective site quickly. These tools use AI to design layouts, generate text content,
and optimize for search engines. Alternatively, use ChatGPT to write website copy by prompting:
“Create homepage content for a tax overage recovery business explaining
what tax overages are and why clients should use my service.” This helps convey your value clearly.
Step 6: Set Up CRM and Workflow Automation Using AI Tools
Managing leads and client communication efficiently is key to success. Free CRM
platforms like HubSpot CRM or Zoho CRM offer AI-powered automation features for tracking
contacts, scheduling follow-ups, and managing pipelines. You can integrate AI chatbots,
such as the free version of ChatGPT plugins or ManyChat, to automate initial client inquiries
on your website or social media pages. Use AI to draft workflow emails or reminders,
for example: “Write a follow-up email template for clients who have not responded to our initial
contact about claiming tax overage funds.” Step 7: Create a Marketing Plan Using AI
To attract clients, you need a strong marketing strategy. Free AI tools can help you generate
ideas, create content, and plan campaigns. Use ChatGPT to brainstorm marketing channels
like local online ads, social media outreach, direct mail, or partnerships with real estate
agents. Prompt ChatGPT: “Develop a 3-month marketing plan for a tax overage business
targeting homeowners in [state]. Include social media, email campaigns, and local advertising.”
You can also use AI to create engaging social media posts and ad copy to boost your reach.
Step 8: Handle Client Claims Process with AI Assistance
Once you start getting clients, you’ll help them file claims for their overage funds. Use AI tools
to prepare documents, forms, and letters quickly. ChatGPT can generate templates or
answer questions about claim paperwork. For instance, prompt: “Generate a checklist and
sample letter for submitting a tax overage claim in [county/state].” This reduces manual effort
and speeds up processing. Step 9: Track Industry
Updates and Competitors Using AI Tax laws and regulations may change,
and keeping up with industry news is crucial. Use AI-powered news aggregators like Feedly
combined with AI summarizers (e.g., ChatGPT) to stay informed without spending hours reading.
Prompt ChatGPT: “Summarize recent changes in tax lien and overage laws in [state].” Also, analyze
competitor websites or marketing strategies using AI SEO tools like Ubersuggest’s free tier to
identify opportunities and threats. Conclusion
Starting a tax overage business can be complex, but leveraging free AI tools can dramatically
simplify research, marketing, communication, and operations. By following these steps—understanding
the business model, gathering data, reaching out to clients, creating an online presence,
automating workflows, marketing effectively, and monitoring performance—you can build a successful
tax overage service. Using AI tools like ChatGPT, free CRM platforms, AI website builders, and data
extraction utilities empowers you to save time and costs, making this niche business more accessible
than ever. With dedication and smart use of AI, you can unlock the value of tax overage
opportunities and build a profitable enterprise. That wraps up the video, Thanks for watching!
If you found it helpful, don’t forget to like and subscribe so you won’t miss future content.

metadata.title: How to Claim Surplus Funds from Foreclosure (Step by Step Tutorial)
metadata.author: Consumer Action Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
We are no longer handling cases related to surplus funds, but feel free to use the video as a resource.

*********************************

How To Claim Surplus Funds From Foreclosure:

In order for there to be surplus funds from a foreclosure sale, the house must have been sold for more than what you owed to the lender.

For example, if you had a loan for $300,000 and your home sold for $500,000 in a foreclosure sale, then a surplus of $200,000 would be remaining, and you could claim that money.

That also means that if your house was sold for less than what you still owed to the lender, there will not be any surplus funds for you to claim.

For example, if your loan was for $500,000 and the home sold for $300,000, there would be nothing remaining to claim after the foreclosure sale.

There are two ways for you to claim surplus funds from a foreclosure. One way is to pursue it yourself and the other way is to go through the process with the help of an attorney.

Method #1
To claim your surplus funds by yourself, you will need to follow these three steps:

➡️ Step 1 is to provide proof of prior ownership. This is done by proving that you are on the title, which can be done by doing a title search.

➡️ Step 2 is to provide verification of funds. You can do this by looking at the foreclosure records and subtracting the loans or liens paid off at the time of the foreclosure sale.

➡️ Step 3 is to contact the trustee. Once you have contacted your trustee, you need to submit a claim form to the trustee and possibly to the court. One thing to note is that if the surplus funds remain unclaimed after 2-3 months, the funds are typically deposited into the court.

Once you have completed these 3 steps, you will be going through the process of hearings & motions with the court and claiming your funds.  You will receive the funds once you submit a successful claim and the court deems that you are the rightful claimant

Method #2
Another option to claim surplus funds is with the help of a surplus funds attorney.

Going through the process with an attorney is very helpful because they will guide you through the process and make sure that everything is done correctly.

When you call my firm, we help you figure out if there’s a surplus right away, with detailed research on title, sale proceeds, the trustee assigned, and the time frame for making a claim with the court.

Now if any of these steps sound confusing to you, don’t worry. It’s not unusual to be confused, especially if it is your first time going through the process.

If you went through foreclosure recently and think you have surplus funds, call us immediately.

Our team will be able to help right away and can also help you find out if you have surplus funds.

metadata.title: How to Start a Surplus Funds Business in 2026 (Step by Step)
metadata.author: Alfred Taren
metadata.shortDescription:
You can start this business with no license, no degree, and without buying a single property. Here's how it actually works, and what your first 30 days should look like.

Surplus funds is the money left over when a property sells at foreclosure auction or tax sale for more than what was owed on it. It's also called excess proceeds, overages, or overbids. The county, the court, or the trustee holds that difference. The former owner is legally entitled to it. And most of the time, nobody ever tells them it exists. That gap is the business.

I've been doing surplus funds recovery since 2013. Over 2,000 cases completed and over $100 million recovered for foreclosure victims across the country. I still run one of the largest surplus recovery operations in the country. I'm not an attorney, I'm not a realtor, and I don't hold a license for any of this.

FREE LIVE MASTERCLASS, every Thursday:
https://surplusfunds.ai

FREE COMMUNITY, my opening script is in there at no charge:
https://skool.com/surplusfunds

CHAPTERS
0:00 The business nobody explains correctly
0:09 Supreme Court proof: Tyler v. Hennepin County
0:47 Who I am: 2,000 cases, no license
1:17 The whole business model in one breath
1:40 Surplus funds vs. state unclaimed property
2:04 The three parts of every deal
2:34 Do you need a license? What a facilitator really is
3:06 What you don't need to start
3:30 The LLC question, and when to actually file
3:52 Fee caps, contact rules, and attorney-only states
5:01 Why most people never close a first deal
6:06 What this costs vs. a franchise or dropshipping
6:42 Starting with nothing: the joint venture path
7:08 Straight talk about the money
7:38 If you work, this works
8:05 Your first 30 days
8:28 How to find county surplus lists on Google
8:52 Two real lists: Marion and Volusia County, FL
9:26 Skip tracing, then picking up the phone
10:18 Fix what broke, then file the LLC
11:17 Free masterclass and free community

THE TWO COUNTY LISTS I PULL UP ON SCREEN
Marion County, FL. Clerk of Court, tax deed surplus funds, updated weekly:
https://www.marioncountyclerk.org/departments/records-recording/tax-deeds-and-lands-available-for-taxes/unclaimed-funds/
Volusia County, FL. Clerk of Court, tax deed surplus list:
https://www.clerk.org/pdf/user_publish/TaxDeeds/Tax_Deed_Surplus_List.pdf

Find your own. Search "surplus funds list" plus the county name, then again with "excess proceeds list" plus the county name. Counties don't all use the same words. Look for the county's own site and skip the paid list sites above it. Not every county posts one. Harris County, Texas publishes nothing.

THE SUPREME COURT CASE
Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023). Decided May 25, 2023, unanimous, Chief Justice Roberts writing. Geraldine Tyler owed roughly $15,000. The county sold her condo for $40,000 and kept all of it. The Court held that keeping the surplus was a taking under the Fifth Amendment.
https://www.supremecourt.gov/opinions/22pdf/22-166_8n59.pdf

COMMON QUESTIONS

What are surplus funds?
Money left over after a property sells at foreclosure auction or tax sale for more than the debt owed on it. Also called excess proceeds, overages, or overbids depending on the state.

Do you need a license to recover surplus funds?
For the work I do, there isn't a license to hold. I'm not an attorney, a realtor, or a private investigator. What changes state to state is your role. Some states cap what you can charge. Some restrict when you can make contact. A few won't let a non-attorney charge a fee at all. In those states you bring in an attorney and quarterback the claim.

How much can you charge?
Caps generally run between 5% and 15% in states that have one. Where there's no cap, fees are negotiated and can go as high as 30%. The cap, if any, is set by state statute.

Do you need an LLC to start?
Eventually yes, and you'll want one. But it isn't step one. File it once you have live prospects and money on the way.

Is this the same as state unclaimed property?
No. State unclaimed property is forgotten bank accounts and utility deposits at the state treasury. Foreclosure and tax sale surplus is different money, a different agency, and different rules.

What does it cost to start?
A laptop, a phone, free public records, and your time. No inventory, no storefront, no employees, no loan.

WHO THIS IS FOR
Wholesalers and investors who keep losing deals to foreclosure or tax sale, and anyone who wants a 100% virtual real estate business with almost no startup cost.

I'm not an attorney and nothing here is legal advice. Statutes, county requirements, fee caps and deadlines are different in every state and they change. Verify the current rules for your state and county before you file anything.

Any income figures I mention are my own results, from my own operation, built over more than a decade with a team. That's my personal experience, not a promise, a projection, or a typical result.

And the longer that they wait, the colder that they get. Ken set up a push alert in his CRM so his phone buzzes the second that somebody replies. Then he jumps on the call right away. That's how Ken closed 23 deals in 6 months and he recovered about $300,000 in total. Okay, so they pick up. Now what do you say and what do you do? These next tips are about the moment you're actually talking to the owner. Tip 16, fix their biggest worry before you even talk about money. Connie's claim it wasn't thinking about his surplus at all. His first conversation was how much time he had left in the house. So he took care of the problem first. People don't hear a word about money while they are scared. They don't know where they're going to sleep. So solving that actually earned his trust. That claim was a $353,000 surplus and Connie made $70,000 on it. Tip 17, don't act like the big boss. Spencer plays the assistant when it's time to talk about the fee. He says, "Hey, I need to talk to my boss." And then he comes back as somebody who's actually on the client's side working to get them a better deal. It turns the fee from a fight into a favor. Spencer's client felt that trust right away and he made $9,500 across two deals this way. Tip 18, Spencer does something else that's also different. When a family is about to lose their home, Spencer helps them negotiate more time to move out using the surplus as collateral so nobody loses money. The buyer gets protected and the family gets breathing room. That can include cash for keys. It can also include extension of stay. Families remember who helped them during the worst months of their lives and the surplus recovery becomes the natural next step. Just make sure an attorney reviews any deal like this before you actually do it. And tip 19, when the phone doesn't work, show up [snorts] with paper. Kenny knocked a door with an agreement form and the printed proof of the sale and that proof is what made it real to the owner. Within 10 minutes, he had an attorney on the phone so the owner could ask questions right there. That was a $128,000 California foreclosure and Kenny made $31,500. Tip 20, trade a small discount for a signature to date. Richard quoted his fee and the owner pushed back so he said, "If you sign right now, I'll come down to 20%." The owner signed on a California deal of over $100,000. Richard made $20,000. 20% of a signed deal beats a higher percentage of nothing. Now, let's get into the part that scares most beginners, the legal side. These tips make it a lot less scary. Tip 21, if the owner has passed away and nobody has opened the probate, open it for them. Without it, no one has the legal right to collect that money. That's real work and it's what justifies a bigger fee. I did this myself on a $210,000 California foreclosure. The family had no will, no trust, no probate so we took care of all of it. My fee was $52,000 which was 25%. Tip 22, put the attorney fees on the client's side of the math. Some claims need an attorney and that cost can eat into your fee if you're not careful. Caesar Santos had his client agree to pay all attorney fees out of the client's share. So Caesar's 20% fee stayed whole. On a $52,000 Florida surplus, he made over $13,000. You can write that into your contract from day one. Tip 23, add a non-circumvention clause to your contract. It says the client can't go around you and file the claim on their own once you've done the work. Rob has that clause inside his contract and he was paid a generous 35% on a North Carolina deal. Have your attorney check the wording for your state. Tip 24, know that your attorney can defend your signed contract. Alvin was working an Indiana claim when somebody else tried to file it. His attorney stepped in, put a stop to it, and the other attorney backed down. A signed contract is only as strong as the person who's willing to stand behind it. That was a $24,000 Indiana surplus claim. Tip 25, if another company already signed the heir, don't walk away yet. Check if they're actually doing anything. Plenty of companies sign people up and then let the file sit. I had a Georgia claim where the heir signed with a company that wasn't actually working the file. I reached out, we came to a settlement, and they actually stalled, and then we had to move the claim again. On that deal, I made $7,276 on a $45,000 sale. Tip 26, learn about summary administration. When an estate is small or the owner passed away a long time ago, a court can skip full probate, and that can cut the time in half. Christian used it on a $138,000 Florida state surplus. The rules change from state to state. So, even if you have an attorney, knowing this tells you what to ask for. All right, last group. This is what happens after the client says yes, and it's where a lot of deals quietly die. Here are four fixes. Tip 27, send your clients to a UPS store. They can print, get it notarized, and ship all in one stop. So, your client doesn't have to hunt for a notary. Danielle did this on a Lake County, Florida claim, and the UPS store mailed the package back to her. She made $17,700. So, she got paperwork signed for her client, and then they refiled. That claim turned into a $44,000 Georgia surplus deal. It was a $5,000 limit on Zelle. So, it took a couple of days. So, tell your client ahead of time how you want to get paid so that nobody panics when the money comes up in pieces. We sent that agreement over and the payout showed up 2 days later. That was an $82,000 payout. And that was all at 30%. If you want to go even further, I made a video showing you how to get ahead of almost every other surplus funds agent out there from my 8 years in this industry. I share how to get to leads before everybody else does, how to reach people when every phone number is dead, and the simple habits that separate the agents who sign deals from the ones who quit. It should be on your screen right now. Click on it and I'll see you there.

metadata.title: Surplus Funds Claim Process Explained (What Nobody Tells You)
metadata.author: Alfred Taren
metadata.shortDescription:
Every surplus funds claim comes down to three questions: who's holding the money, what they require to release it, and how long you have to file. The answers change from state to state — and inside a single state they change again depending on whether the property went to mortgage foreclosure or tax sale.

This is the entire process, start to finish. The three types of office that actually hold the money (plus the fourth that shows up on a timer), form states versus petition states, the exact document package counties require, the four contracts and what each one does, when you need an attorney and when it isn't your choice, and the real filing deadlines by state.

I've been doing surplus funds recovery since 2013 — over 2,000 cases completed, and over $100 million delivered to families across the country.

FREE MASTERCLASS — how the full process runs day to day:
https://surplusfunds.ai

FREE COMMUNITY — come ask questions:
https://skool.com/surplusfunds

CHAPTERS
0:00 Nobody explains what happens after you find a surplus
0:44 The three questions behind every claim
0:59 Step 1: What's actually left after the priority ladder
1:51 Step 2: Who's holding the money — the three buckets
3:41 Form states vs. petition states
4:50 Step 3: Who has the legal right to claim it
5:29 Step 4: The document package counties actually require
8:04 How I run a claim, start to finish
8:43 Step 5: The four contracts, and fee caps
10:03 Step 6: When you need an attorney (and when it isn't your choice)
11:50 California's 90-day no-contact rule
13:34 The honest framework
14:18 Step 7: Filing, and the deadlines by state
15:18 Step 8: Competing claims and getting paid
16:01 Where people actually lose these deals
16:46 Free masterclass, and drop your state below

STATUTES AND SOURCES REFERENCED
Fla. Stat. § 45.032 — clerk holds mortgage foreclosure surplus; 60 days from the certificate of disbursements
Fla. Stat. § 197.582 — clerk holds tax deed surplus; 120 days from the notice date
Tex. Tax Code § 34.04 — excess proceeds by petition; statutory priority order; two-year deadline
Tex. Tax Code § 34.04(i) — attorney fee capped at 25% or $1,000, whichever is less; a non-attorney may not charge a fee to obtain excess proceeds for an owner
Cal. Civ. Code § 2924j — trustee-held surplus after nonjudicial foreclosure; claims due 30 days after notice
Cal. Civ. Code § 2924.21 — 90-day prohibition on contacting a foreclosed-upon homeowner about surplus funds (effective July 18, 2024)
Cal. Rev. & Tax. Code § 4675 — tax-defaulted excess proceeds; one year from recordation of the tax collector's deed
O.C.G.A. § 48-4-5 — excess funds held by the tax commissioner, tax collector, or sheriff; five years before escheat
Ind. Code § 6-1.1-24-7.5 — recovery agreements capped at 10%, must be written and signed, non-compliant agreements invalid
Global Discoveries, Ltd. v. Barnett — a timely claim denied for failure to submit originals before the deadline
Florida Bar UPL advisory opinion (2017), approved by the Florida Supreme Court — non-lawyer surplus recovery and the unlicensed practice of law

WHO THIS IS FOR
Wholesalers and investors who keep losing deals to foreclosure or tax sale, and anyone trying to run surplus funds recovery — excess proceeds, overages, overbids — as an actual business instead of a lottery ticket.

I'm not an attorney and nothing in this video is legal advice. Statutes, county requirements and deadlines change, and they are different in every state. Verify the current rules for your state and your county before you file.

Judicial Mortgage Foreclosures: These are processed through the legal system, often involving sheriff sales or county-held auctions. The process is transparent, with case numbers, dockets, and detailed event sequences accessible to the public. metadata.title: Florida Tax Deed Surplus Claim Forms:  How to Claim Excess Funds
metadata.author: Noble Notary & Legal Document Preparers
metadata.shortDescription:
Did a Florida property sell at a **tax deed auction for more than the taxes, costs, and amounts owed?**

There may be **surplus proceeds** being held by the Clerk of Court.

In this video, I explain the Florida tax deed surplus process under **Florida Statute §197.582**, who may have a claim, the important 120-day rule, and how a Tax Deed Surplus Claim Form is used.

📄 **GET THE FLORIDA TAX DEED SURPLUS CLAIM FORM:**

https://www.floridanotaryservices.org/legal-forms/tax-deed-surplus-claim-form

### What Are Tax Deed Surplus Funds?

When property sells at a Florida tax deed sale for more than the statutory bid and amounts required to satisfy taxes and costs, the excess may become **surplus funds** held for persons with qualifying interests.

Potential claimants may include:

• Former titleholders  
• Mortgage lienholders  
• Judgment lienholders  
• Other qualifying lienholders  
• Personal representatives or successors where applicable

### The 120-Day Rule

This is one of the most important parts.

Florida law generally gives persons receiving the statutory surplus notice **120 days from the notice date to file a written claim**.

For claimants other than the property owner, failing to file a proper claim within that period can permanently bar the claim.

So if you are a lienholder:

### **DO NOT IGNORE THE NOTICE.**

Property-owner claims are treated differently under the statute, so do not assume every claimant has identical deadlines.

### Who Gets Paid First?

Surplus funds are not automatically divided equally.

Florida law requires the Clerk to consider the **priority of valid liens and interests**.

Generally, valid senior liens are addressed before junior liens and before remaining funds are distributed to a former titleholder.

Governmental liens may also receive priority treatment.

### What Does the Claim Include?

Florida’s statutory claim form asks for information such as:

✓ Claimant name and contact information  
✓ Tax deed sale information  
✓ Whether you are a lienholder or titleholder  
✓ Type of lien  
✓ Recording information  
✓ Amount currently due  
✓ Title information  
✓ Amount of surplus claimed  
✓ Homestead status  
✓ Sworn signature

The claim is signed under oath before a **Notary Public or Deputy Clerk**.

### Filing the Claim

Florida law allows a claim to be submitted by methods including:

• U.S. Mail  
• Commercial delivery  
• In person  
• Fax or email when authorized by the Clerk

Always verify the individual county Clerk’s current submission instructions.

### What Happens After Claims Are Filed?

After the statutory claim period ends, the Clerk reviews the claims and may distribute the surplus according to priority.

If competing claims create a dispute, the Clerk may file an **interpleader action** and ask the circuit court to determine who receives the funds.

### What’s Included in Our Form?

✓ Fillable Florida Tax Deed Surplus Claim Form  
✓ Printable PDF  
✓ Titleholder section  
✓ Lienholder section  
✓ Lien and deed-reference fields  
✓ Homestead declaration  
✓ Claim / waiver checkboxes  
✓ Sworn notary section  
✓ Designed for statewide Florida use

📥 **GET THE FLORIDA TAX DEED SURPLUS CLAIM FORM:**

https://www.floridanotaryservices.org/legal-forms/tax-deed-surplus-claim-form

**Fillable PDF • Titleholder + Lienholder sections • Florida §197.582 framework • Statewide use**

**DISCLAIMER:** This form and video are provided for general self-help and educational purposes and are not legal advice. Filing a claim does not guarantee payment. Entitlement depends on title, liens, priority, deadlines, probate issues, and other facts. County Clerk procedures may vary. If ownership or competing claims are disputed, consult a Florida attorney.

#TaxSale

metadata.title: Beginners Guide to Surplus Funds: How to Claim Money After Foreclosure- Step-by-Step Tutorial
metadata.author: Dreams & Dollars: The Everyday Entrepreneur
metadata.shortDescription:
A foreclosure sale may produce more money than is needed to pay the secured debt, taxes, liens, and authorized costs. The remaining excess proceeds are often called surplus funds or foreclosure overages, and eligible parties may be able to claim them.

In this beginner’s guide, Shawn Weeks from Mountain Bay Enterprises explains:
• How surplus funds are created
• Who may have a potential claim, including former owners, heirs, and lienholders
• How to begin searching county and court records
• Common documents and filing steps
• Why liens, priority, deadlines, and competing claims matter
• Warning signs of surplus-funds scams
• When to consult a qualified attorney

Learn more:
https://www.SurplusFundsFinders.net

Instagram:
https://www.instagram.com/mountainbayenterprises

Rules differ significantly by state, county, foreclosure type, and individual case. This video provides general education—not legal, tax, or financial advice—and does not guarantee eligibility, timing, or payment. Confirm current requirements with the government office holding the funds and a qualified attorney in the relevant jurisdiction.

#SurplusFunds #ForeclosureOverages #ExcessProceeds #UnclaimedFunds

segments.text: If you're buying real estate in Texas, there's one thing you absolutely need to do before you close —
and that's check the title.
Texas is one of the hottest real estate markets in the country.
Property values are rising, transactions are moving fast, and the last thing you want is to buy a property
only to find out it comes with someone else's debt attached to it.
So let's talk about liens — what they are, how to find them, and how a title search protects you.
A lien is a legal claim against a property for an unpaid debt.
It can be filed by a lender, a contractor, a court, a homeowners association, the IRS, or a local taxing
authority.
And here's the thing — liens stay with the property, not just the owner.
That means if you buy a property with an unresolved lien, you could be on the hook for it.
There are several types to know about.
Property tax liens arise when property taxes go unpaid.
Mortgage liens are placed by lenders.
Mechanic's liens are filed by contractors who weren't paid for their work.
Judgment liens come from court rulings against the property owner.
HOA liens can be filed for unpaid dues.
And IRS liens cover unpaid federal taxes.
Any one of these can cloud the title and stop a sale from going through.
So how do you find out if a property has liens in Texas?
Here's where to look.
Start with the County Clerk's Office.
Every county in Texas maintains property records — deeds, lien documents, easements, and the full chain
of title.
Most counties have online databases you can search by address or owner name.
Harris County, Travis County, Dallas County — they all have public record portals where this information
lives.
Next, check the County Tax Assessor-Collector's website.
Unpaid property taxes are one of the most common sources of liens, and this is where you'll find out if taxes
are current on the property you're considering.
For court-ordered judgment liens, head to the District or County Clerk.
These can come from lawsuits, unpaid credit card debt, or legal settlements — and they'll be recorded in
the court system.
And for commercial properties, don't forget the Texas Secretary of State.
UCC filings — Uniform Commercial Code liens — apply to business and commercial real estate and are recorded
at the state level.
Now, some of this information is publicly available for free.
But pulling together a complete, accurate picture takes time, access, and expertise.
That's why most investors, lenders, and buyers work with a professional title search company.
Beyond liens, a proper title search also reviews the full chain of title — the chronological history of
every ownership transfer on the property.
Breaks or gaps in that chain can lead to contested ownership or denied title insurance.
You'll also want to check for easements and covenants — legal rights that allow others to use part of the
property, or restrictions that limit what you can do with it.
So what do you do if you find a lien?
First, contact the lienholder — sometimes a lien has been paid but never officially released.
You may be able to negotiate a payoff or settle it at closing.
Once it's resolved, make sure a lien release is filed with the county.
For anything complex or disputed, an attorney or title company can help you navigate it.
The bottom line — buying property in Texas without a title search is a gamble.

the title, checking for liens, and confirming clean ownership is the only way to protect your investment.

lien and deed searches right here in Texas.

metadata.title: How to Find Surplus Funds Lists (Tax Sales and Foreclosures)
metadata.author: Alfred Taren
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people try to find surplus funds one house at a time. That's the slow way. In this video I show you where to find surplus funds leads in bulk using public records, on both the tax sale side and the mortgage foreclosure side, with real examples pulled up on screen.

You'll see three places to look: the county's surplus list for tax sales, the county's online foreclosure auction calendar for court foreclosures, and auction platforms like Auction.com and Xome for foreclosures that don't go through a court. Then I cover the part most people skip: why a big gap between the sale price and the debt isn't surplus yet, the three court documents to look for, and the research every file needs before you make the call.

I'm Alfred Taren. I've been doing surplus funds recovery since 2013, with over 2,000 cases and more than $100 million recovered for foreclosure victims across the country.

FREE LIVE MASTERCLASS (see how we get leads delivered already vetted, researched, and skip traced):
https://surplusfunds.ai

FREE COMMUNITY, 2,000+ people working these deals:
https://skool.com/surplusfunds

WATCH NEXT, how the surplus funds claim process works:
https://youtu.be/ouYE5P3UJdQ

WHO ACTUALLY GETS THE SURPLUS MONEY (liens, owners, and the payout order):
https://youtu.be/SzfjJzM76ls

CHAPTERS
0:00 Stop finding surplus one house at a time
0:30 Who ran the sale holds the money
0:39 Tax sales: the county surplus list
1:44 Court foreclosures: the auction calendar
2:55 The 3 court documents to look for
3:22 No-court foreclosures: Auction.com and Xome
4:02 A big gap isn't surplus yet
4:38 Fresh sales vs old sales
5:08 The honest part
5:23 Recap
5:37 Skip the research: free masterclass
6:19 Next: the first call

COMMON QUESTIONS

Where do I find a surplus funds list?
For tax sales, a lot of counties post a surplus or excess proceeds list right on their website. Search the county name plus "tax deed surplus" or "excess proceeds list" and click the official county result. If they don't post one, a public records request often gets it.

How do I find mortgage foreclosure surplus?
If the foreclosure went through a court, many counties run their foreclosure auctions online on a calendar. Each sale shows the final judgment, which is basically what was owed, and what it sold for. If the foreclosure didn't go through a court, a trustee runs the sale, and a lot of those sales happen on auction platforms like Auction.com and Xome.

What does "third-party bidder" mean on a foreclosure sale?
It means someone other than the lender bought the property. It doesn't tell you there's money left over. Filter twice: third-party sale first, then check whether it sold for more than the judgment.

What court documents show foreclosure surplus?
In the case file, look for the final judgment (what was owed), the certificate of sale (what it sold for), and the certificate of disbursements (what got paid out and what's left).

If a property sold for more than the debt, is there surplus?
Not necessarily. That's a starting point. Second mortgages, other liens, back taxes, and sale costs can come out first, and you still need to confirm who's entitled to what's left.

How do I know if someone already claimed the surplus?
On fresh sales, it's rarely claimed yet. On older sales, check whether a claim's been filed. If the money's been sitting long enough, it may have moved to the state's unclaimed property office.

I'm not an attorney and nothing here is legal advice. Every state's rules are different, and they change. Verify the current law before you act on anything. Results in this business depend on the work you put in.

metadata.title: How to Check for Liens Before You Call About Surplus Funds
metadata.author: Alfred Taren
metadata.shortDescription:
The auction sold for way more than the opening bid, so it looks like a big estimated surplus. But that number might not be the owner's money. Every lien on the property gets its turn first, and if you don't check for them before you call, you could be calling somebody about money that's already spoken for.

In this video I give you a high-level walkthrough of how I check for liens before I ever make that call: what a lien is, the five you'll see most, how a mortgage foreclosure and a tax sale pay liens differently, the three places I look (two of them free), why public records lag behind what's really owed, and the questions I ask the owner.

I'm Alfred Taren. I've been doing surplus funds recovery since 2013, with over 2,000 cases and more than $100 million recovered for foreclosure victims across the country.

FREE LIVE MASTERCLASS, see how the whole process works (and click State Guides at the top to find your state):
https://surplusfunds.ai

FREE COMMUNITY, learn with people already doing this:
https://skool.com/surplusfunds

FREE RESOURCES I MENTION:
NETR Online, a free directory of county record offices: https://publicrecords.netronline.com
Propwire, a free property data site (estimates only): https://propwire.com

WATCH NEXT, your first call to a former homeowner:
https://youtu.be/CqlbwGPmv64

HOW TO FIND SURPLUS FUNDS LISTS:
https://youtu.be/YCb5jYZX_A8

WHO ACTUALLY GETS THE SURPLUS MONEY:
https://youtu.be/SzfjJzM76ls

CHAPTERS
0:00 That number might not be the owner's money
0:41 What a lien is
1:07 The liens you'll see most
1:27 Mortgage foreclosure vs tax sale
2:38 Free state guides
3:01 Three places I check for liens
4:23 Why public records lag behind
4:59 Ask whoever's holding the money
5:17 What I ask the owner
6:16 When it's close
6:58 Recap
7:21 Free masterclass and community

COMMON QUESTIONS

What is a lien?
A lien is a debt that's tied to the property, not just to the person. Common ones are a second mortgage or home equity line, HOA liens, judgment liens, tax liens, and city liens like unpaid water bills or code fines.

Do liens get paid out of surplus funds?
Often, yes. Surplus is what's left after the liens and judgments are paid. On a mortgage foreclosure, the lender that foreclosed is paid first, then the liens that came after it, in order, and the owner gets what's left. A loan recorded before the one that foreclosed usually stays with the house instead.

Does a tax sale wipe out the mortgage?
In a lot of places a tax sale clears other liens off the house, but the lien can move over to the money. The lender can then file a claim to the surplus. A lienholder can lose out if they miss the deadline to file or the money runs out first, and a lender that never got proper notice can keep its loan on the house. Every state handles this differently.

Where can I check for liens for free?
Start with the foreclosure file, then county records (some counties charge, some are free). NETR Online links to county record offices, and free property data sites like Propwire can show what might be on title. Treat those numbers as estimates.

Why isn't the online lien amount the real number?
Interest, penalties, and fees keep adding up, and lenders sometimes add property taxes and insurance they paid. Records are typed in by people, so mistakes happen. The real number comes when the lienholders send their payoffs.

I'm not an attorney and nothing here is legal advice. Every state's rules are different, and they change. Verify the current rules before you act on anything. Always treat amounts as possible funds or estimated surplus. Results in this business depend on the work you put in.

#surplusfunds #excessproceeds #foreclosure

Here's the thing, that number might not be the owner's money, because before the owner sees a dime, every lien on that property gets its turn. And if you don't check those first, you could be calling somebody about money that's already spoken for. So today, I'm going to give you a high level walkthrough on how I check for liens before I make that call. I'm Alfred Taren. I've been doing the surplus funds recovery business since 2013, over 2,000 cases completed and over a hundred million recovered for foreclosure victims across the country. First, what's a lien? This is where a lot of beginners get tripped up. A lien is just a debt that's tied to the property and not just the property tied to the person as well. Here's the line I always come back to. Surplus means that there's something left over after all the liens and judgments are paid. So who pays off those liens? The surplus does. If they're still unpaid, it comes out of the surplus first. Now you don't need to memorize them all, but these are the ones you'll see the most. A second mortgage or a home equity line, HOA liens, judgment liens, which is when somebody sued the owner and won, tax liens from the IRS or state, and city liens like unpaid water bills or code fines. Now here's where it gets interesting. The type of sale changes who gets paid. On a mortgage foreclosure, the lender that foreclosed gets paid first. Then the liens that came after it in order and the owner gets what's left. Now a loan that was recorded before the loan that foreclosed usually isn't paid out of the surplus. it generally stays with the house but not always. Tax sales are a different animal. In a lot of places a tax sale clears the other liens off the house even the mortgage. Now that sounds like the lender just lost right but it's not exactly that way. The liens come off the house but it can move over to the money. So the new buyer gets a clean house and the lender gets in line for the surplus. Same idea as a second mortgage on a regular foreclosure. Now where a lienholder can lose out for good is if they miss the deadline to file, or the money runs out before it's their turn. And sometimes it goes the other way. If the lender never got the notice they were supposed to get, their loan can stay on the house. Then it's not coming out of the surplus at all. Every state handles this a little differently. And that's why I put free guides for all 50 states, including DC, on surplusfunds.ai. Now, whether a tax sale actually wipes out a mortgage for good, that's getting its own video. So stick around. And real quick, don't forget to subscribe, like and comment so you don't miss the next video. Okay, back to business. So where do you actually find these liens? I look in three different places and it depends on what type of sale and where it happened. Number one, the foreclosure file itself. If it went through the court, the lender usually has to name the other lienholders in the lawsuit. So the list of people being sued is basically a lien list. And the final judgment usually shows what the bank was owed with the interest and fees already in there. If it was a trustee sale, start with the notice of sale. Sometimes it'll flat out show you a judgment lien that was recorded against the owner. Number two, county records. Most counties let you search recorded documents by the owner's name. Mortgages, liens, judgments. Some counties charge for it and some are free. If you don't know where your county keeps its records, I have a resource for you. It's called NETR Online. N-E-T-R Online has a free directory that links you to the county record offices across the country. And number three, free property data sites. The one I use is called Propwire and it's free to search. These can show you what might be on title, the first loan, the junior liens, HOA, tax liens, the amounts, and sometimes a possible balance. But that's all estimated so just know that first and don't come to definitive conclusions based on those numbers. And here's why that matters more than people think. Public records don't always catch up to what's really owed. Let's say somebody's been behind six months, twelve months, sometimes longer. The interest, the penalties, and the fees keep stacking up. Sometimes, the lender even pays the property taxes and the insurance to protect the house and it adds all of that to the bill. And remember, humans type these records into the systems themselves, so anytime you give a human a job, there's always going to be room for error. So what you see online is a starting point, not the final answer. So how do you fill in the gaps? By simply asking. Start with whoever is holding the money. the clerk, the trustee or the county can usually tell you what it sold for and how much they're holding. What they usually won't have is what the second mortgage or what the HOA is owed today. That number comes from the lienholder. Then talk to the owner. A lot of times, the truth comes out in the conversation with the homeowner. I'll say something like, "Hey, I'm seeing a couple things pop up on the property. Is that still there or did you pay that off?" If they say they still owe a bunch of money on their second loan, I actually take that seriously and I'll ask them like, "What was the last payoff that you got sent?" And, "How many months were you behind?" If they don't know they can ask the lender for a payoff in writing. If they say They've been outstanding for close to a year or more, you know there's a lot of interest and fees that have piled up and that might not be recorded on public records just yet. So it's always important to ask those questions during the conversation. And just remember. Remember who you're talking to here. This is somebody who just lost their home. They might not even know what that judgment lien is, especially if you're talking to the kids after a parent's passed away. So just be patient. You're there to help them figure out if there's anything left over. Now, what if the numbers are close and you honestly don't know? I don't always just throw it out. I tell the homeowner, "Hey, listen, it doesn't cost you anything to take a look." Then we submit the claim. We can ask for an itemized breakdown of where the money went. The real answer comes when the lienholders send their payoffs. I've had files sit for months waiting on one lienholder who hasn't sent their payoff. And then sometimes we'll see liens that actually don't exist anymore and the surplus can go higher. But it can also go the other way around and the surplus can shrink. metadata.title: Surplus Funds Cold Calling Script: How to Not Sound Like a Scam
metadata.author: Alfred Taren
metadata.shortDescription:
You found the money, you did the math, and you've got a phone number. Now what do you actually say to someone who just lost their house? In this video I walk you through the exact way I open a first call to a former homeowner, on both mortgage foreclosures and tax sales.

You'll hear how I open with the auction results instead of "surplus funds," how to walk through the numbers without overpromising, what to do when they ask "is this a scam?", how to handle "I need to think about it," when to bring up the fee, and how to book the next step before you hang up. I also cover what to say when the owner's passed away and you're talking to family, and why most deals come from follow-up, not the first try.

I'm Alfred Taren. I've been doing surplus funds recovery since 2013, with over 2,000 cases and more than $100 million recovered for foreclosure victims across the country.

FREE PHONE SCRIPT (download it inside our free community):
https://www.skool.com/surplusfunds/classroom/1c7fa543?md=8ff95ab8ef5042268cfd1911c7c5e20c

FREE COMMUNITY, practice with people already making these calls:
https://skool.com/surplusfunds

FREE LIVE MASTERCLASS (see how the whole business works, plus the tools and processes I use):
https://surplusfunds.ai

WATCH NEXT, how to find surplus funds lists:
https://youtu.be/YCb5jYZX_A8

CAN HEIRS CLAIM SURPLUS FUNDS (when the owner's passed away):
https://youtu.be/Jt5CmG8sjq4

HOW SURPLUS FUNDS AGENTS GET PAID:
https://youtu.be/dgyIbUV-P7s

CHAPTERS
0:00 What to say on your first surplus funds call
0:37 Before you dial: numbers and rules
1:27 How I open the call
2:05 Walking through the numbers
2:48 "Is this a scam?"
3:31 Your tone matters more than your words
3:56 "I need to think about it"
4:30 When to bring up the fee
4:44 Book the next step
5:12 When the owner's passed away
5:57 Make every connected call count
6:18 If they don't pick up
6:54 Recap
7:14 Free phone script and masterclass

COMMON QUESTIONS

What do I say when I call a former homeowner about surplus funds?
Don't open with "surplus funds." Open with the auction results: who you are, the property, and that it looks like it sold. Ask if they have a moment to go over the numbers, then pause and let them talk.

How do I explain the surplus without overpromising?
Walk through what it sold for and roughly what was owed, and use words like "possible," "could," and "might." Don't promise a number on the first call.

What if they ask "is this a scam?"
Don't argue. Show them. Send the public auction listing so they can see the sale for themselves, and walk through the math again.

What if the former owner has passed away?
You're now talking to family. Be respectful, find out who you're speaking with (spouse, child, executor), and ask whether anyone's started probate. Being family isn't the same as having the right to claim.

When can I call, and what rules apply?
Federal rules limit calls to between 8 a.m. and 9 p.m. in the person's local time. Stop calling anyone who asks you to, don't use robocalls or autodialers on cell phones without the right permission, and check whether there's a waiting period after the sale before you're allowed to contact the owner where you're working.

What if they don't answer?
That's normal. Leave a short voicemail, send a short text, and keep following up. Most deals don't come from the first try.

I'm not an attorney and nothing here is legal advice. Every state's rules are different, and they change. Verify the current law before you act on anything. Results in this business depend on the work you put in.

#surplusfunds #excessproceeds #foreclosuresurplus

metadata.title: Why Most Surplus Funds Calls Fail (And What To Say Instead)
metadata.author: Surplus Funds Secrets
metadata.shortDescription:
Most people think surplus funds cold calls are just another version of regular sales calls.

They're not.

In fact, treating surplus funds calls like traditional cold calls is one of the fastest ways to destroy good leads and lose trust before the conversation even starts.

In most industries, you're calling to sell something.

Real estate. Insurance. Solar. Marketing. Credit repair.

In surplus funds, you're calling to inform someone that they may be owed a significant amount of money connected to a foreclosure, tax sale, or estate.

That sounds easier.

It's not.

Because you're asking someone to trust a complete stranger who's calling them about money they didn't even know existed.

In this video, I break down the psychology behind surplus funds calls, why traditional sales scripts often fail, and how to structure conversations that build trust instead of resistance.

Topics covered:

• Why surplus funds calls are different from traditional cold calls
• The psychology claimants experience during the first conversation
• Common mistakes that immediately destroy trust
• Why language and wording matter so much
• The difference between sounding like a salesperson and sounding like a professional
• How to establish legitimacy from the first few seconds of the call
• The role of education, clarity, and trust in the recovery process
• Why preparation beats pressure every time

The reality is that most claimants are hearing this information for the very first time.

They're skeptical.

They're confused.

And many of them assume it's a scam.

Your job isn't to "close" them immediately.

Your job is to provide clarity, explain the process, answer questions, establish credibility, and help them understand what happened and what options may be available.

The operators who understand this consistently outperform those who rely on generic sales tactics.

Because surplus funds isn't about pressure.

It's about trust.

Surplus funds cold calling demands a delicate balance of empathy and clarity to unlock money owed from foreclosure tax sales and estates.

This video discusses how to shift cold calling scripts from sales-heavy to trust-focused communication that immediately addresses prospects’ concerns and builds legitimacy.

Learn how to reframe language to avoid triggering fear or suspicion and how to explain next steps professionally while offering convenience.

For professionals handling surplus funds recovery or distressed real estate leads, mastering these techniques elevates client engagement and conversion.

Watch to gain insight into crafting effective surplus funds calls and encourage ethical, empathetic outreach.

Like this video and comment “SURPLUS” below
I’ll send you a free e-book that dives deep into this.

For those of you who don't know, surplus funds is when a foreclosed home sells way more than what it was worth, and that extra money sits in a government account waiting to be claimed by the previous owner, which most of the time they have no idea it's there. And you can help them claim it for a fee. Sometimes that fee can be thousands of dollars for you. But the funds don't last forever. They'll usually get absorbed into the state or county treasury after a certain amount of time. And it depends which state you are working from. With Texas, you have about two years to reclaim this excess funds. Florida, you have one. Georgia, you have five. And remember, the clock starts as soon as the sale closes, not as soon as the owner finds out about the money. So, let's say you found a $15,000 claim with eight months left until the time is up. You contact the owner, you fill out some paperwork for them, and you take your cut of anywhere between 10% to 50%. All for a few phone calls and some paperwork. Don't just sit on it until there's like 30 or 60 days left because claims typically take 30 to 90 days to process depending on how busy the state is. metadata.title: How do I recover surplus funds after a reverse-mortgage foreclosure? | NC
metadata.author: Pierce Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Q: How do I recover surplus money after a reverse-mortgage foreclosure sale when the property belonged to an estate?

A: Surplus is the money left after the foreclosure sale pays the sale costs, any required taxes or assessments, and the reverse-mortgage payoff. When the homeowner has died, the surplus is usually treated as an estate asset. If the trustee or sale officer cannot safely determine who should receive it, the surplus is often paid into the office of the Clerk of Superior Court in the county where the sale happened. In most cases, the estate’s qualified personal representative, meaning the executor or administrator, is the right person to claim those funds for the estate. The personal representative typically files a request with the clerk to release the surplus, and provides proof of authority such as Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration, along with information that ties the funds to the foreclosure file. If the clerk agrees there is one proper payee, the clerk can enter an order disbursing the money to the estate. If there are competing claims, like heirs disagreeing or a creditor claiming the funds, the clerk may require a special proceeding to decide who is legally entitled to the surplus and then issue a disbursement order. After the estate receives the money, the personal representative deposits it into the estate account, pays allowed estate expenses and valid claims in the required order, and only then distributes what remains to the heirs or beneficiaries. Timing can depend on when the sale becomes final, including any upset bid period, and when the trustee completes the final accounting.

metadata.title: Who Gets Surplus Funds After a Foreclosure or Tax Sale? (It's Not Who You Think).
metadata.author: Alfred Taren
metadata.shortDescription:
A big number on a surplus list isn't what the homeowner gets. Here's who actually gets paid from surplus funds after a mortgage foreclosure or a tax sale, in plain English, with real numbers.

Surplus funds, also called excess proceeds or overages, is the money left over after a property sells at auction for more than what was owed. But it doesn't all go to the former owner. Anyone with a claim on the house, like a second mortgage, an unpaid HOA, or an old judgment, usually gets paid first. The homeowner is at the back of the line.

I'm Alfred Taren. I've been doing surplus funds recovery since 2013, with over 2,000 cases and more than $100 million recovered for foreclosure victims across the country.

FREE LIVE MASTERCLASS:
https://surplusfunds.ai

FREE COMMUNITY, 2,000+ people working these deals:
https://skool.com/surplusfunds

WATCH FIRST, tax sale surplus vs foreclosure surplus:
https://youtu.be/9TIsznbRNRk

CHAPTERS
0:00 A $180,000 surplus that isn't what it looks like
0:20 Who actually gets the money?
0:43 Surplus is what's left after everyone in line gets paid
1:20 Mortgage foreclosure example: $180,000 becomes $55,000
2:12 Tax sale example: $60,000 surplus, homeowner gets $0
2:58 The good news: the line can get shorter
3:24 When the owner passed away, the family can still claim
4:10 Three things to check before you call
4:55 Recap and free resources

COMMON QUESTIONS

Who gets surplus funds after a foreclosure?
Usually not just the homeowner. After the foreclosing lender is paid, other people with a claim on the house, like a second mortgage, an HOA, or someone with a court judgment, generally get paid from the surplus first. The former owner gets what's left.

Who gets surplus funds after a tax sale?
Same idea. In a lot of states, the tax sale clears the mortgage off the house, but the mortgage company can file a claim on the surplus and get paid before the former owner. If the mortgage is bigger than the surplus, the owner can end up with nothing.

Does the homeowner always get the surplus?
No. In most states the former owner is last in line. The number on a surplus list is the starting number, not what the owner walks away with.

Can the surplus amount go up?
Sometimes. In some states, people in line have to file a claim by a deadline. If they don't, they can lose their spot, and more money moves down to the owner.

What happens to surplus funds if the owner passed away?
In most states the right to claim passes to the family, like a spouse, children, or sometimes siblings. They'll usually need a death certificate and proof they're the heirs, and sometimes a probate case.

What should I check before calling about a surplus?
Three things. Look at the actual case or sale file to see what's been paid. Look up everything recorded against the house. And make sure you're calling the right person.

I'm not an attorney and nothing here is legal advice. Rules differ by state and county and they change. Verify the current rules in your state before you file anything. Results in this business depend on the work you put in.

What happens after a surplus funds claimant signs your agreement?

Getting someone to say YES is a big step—but the work doesn’t stop there. In fact, what you do after the agreement is signed can make a huge difference in how smoothly the surplus funds recovery process moves forward.

In this video, we’ll walk through what happens after a claimant signs, including the next steps you should take, how to keep the claimant informed, how to stay organized, and how to avoid dropping the ball after getting the YES.

If you’re building a surplus funds recovery business, this video will help you understand what to do after closing a surplus funds lead and how to create a simple process for moving each claimant to the next step.

In this video:

What happens after a surplus funds claimant signs
What to do immediately after getting a signed agreement
How to follow up after closing a surplus funds lead
How to keep your claimant informed
How to stay organized during the surplus funds recovery process
Common mistakes to avoid after getting the YES
How a CRM can help you track every step

You found a surplus funds lead…

You can't find the person. 😂

In this video, I'll show you how to skip trace surplus funds leads and find better contact information for the people you may need to reach.

You'll learn:

✅ How to make sure you're skip tracing the RIGHT person

✅ Common mistakes beginners make when skip tracing surplus funds leads

The goal isn't to collect a giant list of phone numbers.

5 Critical Steps to Get Paid from Surplus Funds

metadata.title: Can I use a finder's-fee agreement to claim unclaimed funds? | NC
metadata.author: Pierce Law Group
metadata.shortDescription:
Q: Can I use a finder's-fee agreement to help people claim unclaimed funds held by the state?

A: Yes — but only if you follow strict rules. A finder's-fee agreement can be void and unenforceable if it is signed too early, charges too much, or leaves out required disclosures and notarized signatures. In many cases, the owner should use the state's claim process first. If the matter involves heirs, estate authority, disputed ownership, or competing claims, a simple template may not be enough, and a court process may be required instead. There is also a timing rule — these agreements generally cannot be signed during the first twenty-four months after the property is paid or delivered to the state, unless the agreement is with an attorney for a claim or special proceeding involving identified property or to challenge a denial. Fees are also limited by law, often to the lesser of one thousand dollars or twenty percent of the amount recovered. And before a property finder starts a claim, that person may need to be registered with the Treasurer and licensed as a private investigator. So the short answer is yes, but only with careful compliance — and not every unclaimed-funds case can be handled with a standard finder's-fee contract.

metadata.shortDescription:
1. What Are Tax Sale Surplus Funds? When a property gets sold at a tax auction for more than what’s owed in taxes, the extra cash is called surplus funds. If someone owes $10,000 in taxes but the property sells for $50,000, there’s $40,000 in surplus. That money doesn’t belong to the government; it belongs to the former property owner.

But here's the catch: many homeowners don’t even know this cash exists, and that's where recovery agencies step in.

2. Why Homeowners Don’t Claim Their Funds

Lack of knowledge: Many have no idea surplus funds are waiting for them.
Confusion over legal processes: The rules can be tricky, and some think it's impossible to get the funds back.
Time limits: There are deadlines for claiming these funds, and if they miss the window, they lose it forever.
3. How a Quality Recovery Agency Helps Your job is to find these unclaimed surplus funds and connect with homeowners who might otherwise lose out. A good agency does the legwork, filing paperwork and ensuring clients get their cash. You get a cut, they get their money, and everyone wins.

4. Steps for Recovery

Find the surplus funds: Scour government databases and public records to locate surplus from tax sales.
Track down the homeowner: Sometimes this means chasing leads or using skip tracing services to locate people who’ve moved or disappeared.
File the claim: Each state has its own process for claiming surplus funds. Fill out the right paperwork and submit it within the deadlines.
Get paid: Once you’ve successfully helped someone recover their funds, you take an agreed-upon fee or percentage.
5. Legalities and Red Tape Each state has different laws regarding surplus funds, so you’ll need to know:

Timeframes: How long after a sale can a homeowner claim the funds?
Fees: Many states cap how much recovery agencies can charge, usually between 10% and 30%.
Documentation: Some states require notarized affidavits, while others have less formal requirements.
6. Marketing Your Recovery Services Most people have no idea recovery agencies exist. To reach them:

Run targeted ads: Focus on homeowners in areas with frequent tax sales.
Cold calling and direct mail: Once you’ve identified potential clients, reach out directly. But be mindful of local regulations on solicitation.
Word of mouth: The best clients come from referrals. Help one person get their surplus, and word will spread.
7. Challenges You’ll Face

Skepticism: People might think it’s a scam. Be transparent about your services and fees to build trust.
Competition: Other recovery agencies might already be working the same area. Make sure your pitch stands out by focusing on how smooth and fast you can make the process for them.
Legal roadblocks: Sometimes the paperwork can get tangled in red tape, or a judge might deny a claim due to a missed deadline or error in the documentation.
8. Pro Tips for Recovery Agencies

Stay organized: Keep track of deadlines and cases so you don’t miss out on potential claims.
Learn the laws: Each state’s rules are different, so specialize in the states you’re most comfortable working in.
Build relationships: Networking with real estate agents, lawyers, and tax professionals can lead to more referrals.
Helping homeowners recover their lost tax sale surplus funds is not just about the money; it’s about providing a service that can change lives.

10%. That is the number you absolutely

written disclosure explicitly telling

legal documentation. So, no more trying

action.

standard, not the exception.

nation is just undeniable at this point.

consumer protections that could
completely lock out unprepared
businesses.

to just pass their own versions. This is
your blueprint for the future, no matter

Which brings us to section four, the

segments.text: You just closed a really good surplus
funds client with $45,000 in surplus.
But after everything was done, the
county only released $9,000.
Now, the client wants the money that was
promised to him. You don't know how
$9,000 will cover your fees and all of
your effort is flushed down the drain.
Not to mention, now you have an angry
client who thinks you ripped him off.
This is a classic misunderstanding that
happens all the time while working in
surplus funds. You see, the $45,000 you
saw on that surplus funds list never
belonged to your client in the first
place. Most of that money belonged to
those standing in line ahead of your
client. These people are called the
competing lien holders. And today, I am
going to tell you how they affect
surplus funds claims. How to check for
them before you file and how to protect
your client from finding out too late.
First of all, you need to stop looking
at the surplus amount as the final
payout because that number is only what
was left after the sale and it doesn't
automatically mean the former homeowner
receives all of it. The thing is, when
someone owes a debt, whether it's unpaid
taxes, a mortgage, HOA fees, or a court
judgment, the creditor can file a lien
against their property as a legal
guarantee. Now, if the property is ever
sold, they get paid from the proceeds
before the owner sees a dollar. It's
essentially the law's way of making sure
debts don't just disappear when a
property changes hands.
These people are usually the ones who
get to keep their money from the surplus
funds before the original homeowner gets
anything back from the county. Now, the
priority order varies by state and sale
type, but the basic idea is consistent.
First in line are property taxes and
government claims, which almost always
come before everything else. After that,
you have IRS federal tax liens, then
municipal assessments like unpaid
utilities or code violations, then HOA
claims, then the first mortgage, the
second mortgage, and judgment liens from
creditors or court rulings. The former
owner only gets what's left or every
valid claim ahead of them is cleared.
So, if the surplus is $45,000,
but there are $36,000 in valid claims
sitting ahead of your client, the real
conversation is about $9,000, not
That is exactly why you never promise
the full number. You explain from day
one that the county may need to satisfy
other legal claims before releasing the
final amount.
Now, IRS liens need their own attention
because a lot of agents assume the
property sale wipes everything out, and
it doesn't always work that way.
If you see a federal tax lien, you need
to verify whether it was properly filed,
whether it still attaches to the
proceeds, and whether the IRS has a
right to claim from the surplus. This is
one of those spots where a real estate
attorney or tax lien professional can
save the case before you create a bigger
problem. And here is how you avoid
getting there in the first place. Run
the lien search before you sign the
client. For this, you can start with the
county recorder or clerk records and
search the parcel number, the property
address, and the previous homeowner's
full legal name. Look for mortgages,
deeds of trust, HOA liens, municipal
liens, mechanics liens, judgments, or
anything recorded against the property.
Then, check for federal tax liens
separately. And don't just search the
property address, search the owner's
name, too, because some liens follow the
person and won't show up in a property
search. After that, run a judgment
search through your state court portal,
and use PACER, the Public Access to
Court Electronic Records website, if
there could be federal judgments
involved. This doesn't have to take all
day. Once you get used to it, even 20
minutes of checking can save you from
signing a case that was never going to
pay the way you thought. But, what if a
lien holder shows up after you file?
Don't panic because a lien holder filing
a claim doesn't automatically mean your
client gets nothing. It means the
county, clerk, or court has to determine
who gets paid and in what order. Your
job is to verify the claim, request a
written payoff statement, check whether
the lien amount matches the records, and
look at whether extra fees have been
tacked on. HOA claims especially can
grow fast with attorney fees, collection
costs, and late charges. And if the
number looks inflated, get it in writing
and have the client challenge it through
the proper process if the state allows
that. I'll make another video on exactly
how to do that. For now, just know when
the file needs legal help, it's not
always a bad deal. However, I would
suggest not signing clients where the
competing lien holders take more than
40% of the surplus amount. But, if you
do commit to a case like this, keep a
paper trail from day one. Certified
mail, email records, payoff requests,
notes from phone calls, copies of every
document you send. If a lien holder was
notified and missed the claim window,
your documentation is what protects the
disbursement later.

These people are usually the ones who get to keep their money from the surplus funds before the original homeowner gets anything back from the county. Now, the priority order varies by state and sale type, but the basic idea is consistent. First in line are property taxes and government claims, which almost always come before everything else. After that, you have IRS federal tax liens, then municipal assessments like unpaid utilities or code violations, then HOA claims, then the first mortgage, the second mortgage, and judgment liens from creditors or court rulings. The former owner only gets what's left or every valid claim ahead of them is cleared. So, if the surplus is $45,000, but there are $36,000 in valid claims sitting ahead of your client, the real conversation is about $9,000, not $45,000. That is exactly why you never promise the full number. You explain from day one that the county may need to satisfy other legal claims before releasing the final amount. Now, IRS liens need their own attention because a lot of agents assume the property sale wipes everything out, and it doesn't always work that way. If you see a federal tax lien, you need to verify whether it was properly filed, whether it still attaches to the proceeds, and whether the IRS has a right to claim from the surplus. This is one of those spots where a real estate attorney or tax lien professional can save the case before you create a bigger problem. And here is how you avoid getting there in the first place. Run the lien search before you sign the client. For this, you can start with the county recorder or clerk records and search the parcel number, the property address, and the previous homeowner's full legal name. Look for mortgages, deeds of trust, HOA liens, municipal liens, mechanics liens, judgments, or anything recorded against the property. Then, check for federal tax liens separately. And don't just search the property address, search the owner's name, too, because some liens follow the person and won't show up in a property search. After that, run a judgment search through your state court portal, and use PACER, the Public Access to Court Electronic Records website, if there could be federal judgments involved. This doesn't have to take all day. Once you get used to it, even 20 minutes of checking can save you from signing a case that was never going to pay the way you thought. But, what if a lien holder shows up after you file? Don't panic because a lien holder filing a claim doesn't automatically mean your client gets nothing. It means the county, clerk, or court has to determine who gets paid and in what order. Your job is to verify the claim, request a written payoff statement, check whether the lien amount matches the records, and look at whether extra fees have been tacked on. HOA claims especially can grow fast with attorney fees, collection costs, and late charges. And if the number looks inflated, get it in writing and have the client challenge it through the proper process if the state allows that. I'll make another video on exactly how to do that. For now, just know when the file needs legal help, it's not always a bad deal. However, I would suggest not signing clients where the competing lien holders take more than 40% of the surplus amount. But, if you do commit to a case like this, keep a paper trail from day one. Certified mail, email records, payoff requests, notes from phone calls, copies of every document you send. If a lien holder was notified and missed the claim window, your documentation is what protects the disbursement later. Know who's ahead of your client. Unclaimed property vs. foreclosure surplus funds — are they the same thing? Not quite, and knowing the difference could matter if money is connected to your name.
In this video, we break down:

🔹 What unclaimed property actually is (old bank accounts, uncashed checks, insurance payments, security deposits, utility refunds)

🔹 What foreclosure surplus funds are (leftover money after a foreclosure sale pays off debt, liens, and costs)

🔹 Where each type of fund is held — state unclaimed property offices vs. courts, sheriffs, trustees, or county offices

🔹 Why the claims process, required documents, and deadlines can be completely different depending on which type you're dealing with

segments.text: You may have heard the terms unclaimed property and foreclosure surplus funds
used interchangeably. But they’re not the same — and knowing the difference
can matter if money is connected to your name. Today we’re breaking down what each one means,
where the money comes from, and why the claiming process isn’t always the same. One of the biggest
reasons funds go unclaimed is simple: people don’t know what type of money it is — or where to start.
Let’s start with unclaimed property. Unclaimed property usually refers to financial
assets that were left behind or forgotten — things like old bank accounts, uncashed checks, insurance
payments, security deposits, or utility refunds. When a company or financial institution can’t
locate the owner after a required period, it may have to turn those funds over to the state.
The state then holds the money until the rightful owner or heir comes forward to claim it.
Now, foreclosure surplus funds are different. These can happen when a foreclosed property
sells for more than the amount needed to pay the mortgage debt,
taxes, liens, and sale-related costs. Any remaining balance may belong to
the former homeowner or another party with a legal right to it.
In many places, those funds are held by a court, sheriff, trustee, or county office rather than the
state unclaimed property program. So what’s the real difference?
Unclaimed property usually comes from financial accounts or business records and is commonly
handled through a state unclaimed property office. Foreclosure surplus funds come from the sale
of a foreclosed property and are usually claimed through the court
or local office handling the case. Both may require proof of identity,
ownership, or inheritance, but the process and deadlines can be very different.
That’s why it’s important to know which type of funds you may be dealing with — because
that determines where to look, what documents to gather, and how much time you may have.
That’s where understanding the difference becomes critical.
