Welcome to this Surplus Funds Recovery training! In this video, I’m going to show you an incredible real estate strategy that not many people know about—surplus funds. If you've heard about real estate through agents, flippers, or landlords, you're about to discover a new way to profit by helping people recover money left behind after foreclosures. This is the same strategy that has transformed my life and the lives of hundreds of my students.

Hi, I’m Eric Richardson. After playing professional basketball in Europe, I transitioned into the surplus funds business in 2018, and now run a six-figure asset recovery company. Through my business, Prestige Family Assets Group, I’ve helped countless people claim their surplus funds, while also coaching students on how to build a profitable business doing the same.

In this video, I’ll break down exactly what surplus funds are, how foreclosures lead to this hidden money, and how YOU can help individuals and businesses recover these funds for a percentage of the payout. I’ll walk you through the process of finding surplus funds (which is public information!), contacting the rightful owners, and getting paid when they get paid. Plus, I’ll share real-life success stories from students who’ve claimed amounts as large as $557,000!

I’ll also explain the different ways you can get started, including enrolling in my detailed course, joining group training, or even letting me set up the business for you with a full team and system in place.

Ready to change your financial future by helping people recover the money they didn’t know they had? Watch this webinar, take notes, and let’s get started on this journey together! 💰

metadata.title: How to Start an Asset Recovery Business | Surplus Funds & 90-Day Business Mentorship
metadata.author: Hutch & Holmes
metadata.shortDescription:
Are you interested in starting an asset recovery business but don't know where to begin?

In this video, Nekia with Hutch & Holmes explains how the asset recovery business works, how foreclosure surplus funds are identified, and the steps you can take to start building your own business.

I specialize in helping homeowners identify and pursue surplus funds from **mortgage foreclosures and tax foreclosures**. I also help aspiring Asset Recovery Advocates learn how to build a business providing this service.

**WHAT YOU'LL LEARN:**
- What an asset recovery business is
- What foreclosure surplus funds are
- How mortgage and tax foreclosure surplus funds work
- Why former homeowners may not know funds are available
- The FIND → INFORM → ASSIST business process
- How to research surplus claim procedures in your state
- Why understanding the claimant's process comes first
- How to work with me through the FREE Facebook Community or 90-Day Business Mentorship Program

Timestamp
0:00 Welcome & Introduction
0:56 Why Information Alone Isn't Enough
1:45 What Is an Asset Recovery Business?
2:08 Mortgage & Tax Foreclosure Surplus Funds
2:49 Why Homeowners May Not Know About Surplus
3:56 FIND → INFORM → ASSIST
5:45 How Asset Recovery Advocates May Get Paid
6:15 Research the Surplus Claim Process
8:39 Join the Free Community
9:27 90-Day Business Mentorship


**YOUR FIRST ACTION STEP**

Choose one county and state where you want to work. Research how a homeowner would claim mortgage foreclosure surplus funds and tax foreclosure surplus funds separately.

Understanding the claim process helps you determine what services your asset recovery business may legally provide.

**TWO WAYS TO WORK WITH ME**

💙 **1. FREE FACEBOOK COMMUNITY + ASSET RECOVERY BUSINESS GUIDE**

Join our community of aspiring and growing Asset Recovery Advocates for monthly LIVE Q&A sessions, training, resources, and business-building guidance.

👉 Join the Facebook Community: 
https://www.facebook.com/groups/2219434898892098

👉 Get the Asset Recovery Business Guide: 
https://hutchandholmes.gumroad.com/l/business-guide-for-beginners

💛 **2. HUTCH & HOLMES 90-DAY BUSINESS MENTORSHIP**

Looking for personalized, one-on-one support?

My 90-Day Mentorship Program is designed to help you get started, understand the business process, create an action plan, and begin building your asset recovery business with guidance and accountability.

📲 Text **MENTORSHIP** to **321-710-7176** to learn more.

**ABOUT HUTCH & HOLMES**

Hutch & Holmes helps aspiring Asset Recovery Advocates move beyond simply learning about surplus funds to taking practical steps toward building an asset recovery business.

**Don't just learn the business. Build the business.**

Let's build your asset recovery business—together!

*Educational information only. Surplus funds claim procedures, third-party assistance rules, licensing requirements, and compensation restrictions vary by state and claim type. Results and income are not guaranteed.*

------------------------------------------

metadata.title: Owed money in someone's bankruptcy? The free federal court search
metadata.author: Held
metadata.shortDescription:
https://ucf.uscourts.gov/

Were you owed money in someone's bankruptcy? Bankruptcy courts hold money creditors never collected, and the search is free. U.S. Courts still run the Unclaimed Funds Locator, a public search for money held by participating bankruptcy courts. This is not financial advice. I am not a finder. I am not telling you that you are owed money. Searching the official locator is free. Do not pay anyone to run a search you can run yourself. This video does not enter a Social Security number and does not file a claim.

Official:
https://ucf.uscourts.gov/
https://ucf.uscourts.gov/about
https://www.usa.gov/unclaimed-money
https://www.uscourts.gov/forms-rules/forms/application-payment-unclaimed-funds

Facts from those pages (verified Sep 1, 2026, America/Denver):
- Live URL that actually loaded: https://ucf.uscourts.gov/ (HTTP 200, no redirect). Title: "Unclaimed Funds Locator." Heading: U.S. Courts Unclaimed Funds Locator. No last-updated stamp on the search page. Footer: Version 3.03e, © 2015-2026 US Courts, Collaboratively Developed Software (VAEB).
- USA.gov unclaimed-money table, last updated September 24, 2025, row "Bankruptcies": "Use the U.S. Courts Unclaimed Funds Locator to search for money you may be owed after a person or business declared bankruptcy." The USA.gov href is https://ucf.uscourts.gov/.
- Search form (live): Court dropdown placeholder "Select Court(s) Or Leave Empty For All Courts" (83 options loaded). Creditor Name* and Debtor Name* (placeholders "Search By Creditor Name" / "Search By Debtor Name"). Case Number (max 20). Entered On or After. Image CAPTCHA. Buttons: Clear, Search. On-page note: either Creditor Name or Debtor Name must have a minimum of 3 characters. No Social Security field.
- About (https://ucf.uscourts.gov/about): collaborative locator for Bankruptcy Court unclaimed funds; JFinSys from Virginia Eastern Bankruptcy Court; courts opt in. Search one district, several, or all participating courts. Names are full-text indexes. CAPTCHA required to search. Court Specific Information directory: 85 districts plus All Courts (86 items), including COB - Colorado Bankruptcy Court.
- Demo: fake creditor name Jane Example (not a viewer), court set to COB. Search without solving CAPTCHA returned "Incorrect Captcha." No results table. Address modal not opened. This video does not file a claim. Form 1340 on uscourts.gov is a template; a claim, if any, is filed with the court that holds the funds (Colorado about-page line points to https://www.cob.uscourts.gov for disposition requirements).

#USCourts #UnclaimedFunds #bankruptcy

segments.text: Hello Everyone, Welcome back to our Video Updates. It's Sade.
Today's video is going to cover the question relating to Junior Lienholders and what happens
when there are excess proceeds from a foreclosure sale, but there are some Junior Lienholders. So,
typically this question comes in the context of a homeowner that, a homeowner whose property
went to foreclosure sale because of failure to pay property taxes. And let's say that that homeowner
was not paying the property taxes but also had a mortgage on the home, and possibly was paying the
mortgage so the mortgage lender didn't really notice about the property taxes. It's possible
sometimes because not everybody pays their property taxes through their mortgage payments.
So let's say that the tax office in that county went ahead and did a foreclosure ,but there was
still a mortgage loan hanging out there on that property, that means that the collateral is gone.
Right? The tax office sold the property off so that the mortgage is still there which is
the debt obligation but the collateral that was securing that loan is gone. So then, the question
is "What happens at that point if there are excess proceeds left over from the sale"? So, let's say
I had a piece of property and I was paying on the property as far as my mortgage payments but
somehow I wasn't able to pay my tax payments, and then the county took the property and sold it. So,
the property in this example let's say it was sold for two hundred thousand dollars but I only
owed ten thousand dollars on my taxes. So then, there's $190,000 left over which we call excess
proceeds. Right? So the excess proceeds rightfully belong to someone. They don't belong to the county
unless the claim period has completely expired and the claim period in Texas for those types
of sales is two years. So, that money a hundred and ninety thousand dollars belongs to someone
but who exactly? So that's what this question is trying to figure out. It belongs to several
people in order of priority according to the Tax Code. And so it will belong to
some other taxing agencies that might have been owed money but they didn't
get that money right before the sale, so they could still put in a petition and collect the
taxes owed. It also could belong to the mortgage lender because the mortgage lender's debt is still
hanging out there even though there's no longer a collateral for it. So let's say I still owed
on my mortgage a hundred thousand dollars at the time that that tax foreclosure happened,
then that means that the mortgage lender could apply to get a hundred thousand dollars from those
excess proceeds, and then I will get the remaining ninety thousand dollars. That's how it works.
Now, what if I as the property owner would like to claim all of the hundred and ninety thousand
dollars, can I do that? So that's the related question that people want to know. And the answer
is Yes. You can definitely do that. There are certain procedural steps that have to be taken
and there's a risk that in future, potentially that mortgage lender might come after you for
deficiency on the mortgage loan. I don't think they will be successful and the reason why
is because there are certain steps in the process where the parties are required to
notify the mortgage lender and if they did that correctly, then the mortgage lender failed to
claim the money on time. So that's their loss. So, typically they have a notice that's sent out by
the county's lawyers when the tax foreclosure lawsuit is filed. It will be sent out to me
as a homeowner, it will also be sent out to my mortgage lender to let them know this is going on,
if I still have a mortgage on that home. And then that's the time frame in which the mortgage lender
has the opportunity to contest the sale, you know, pay off the property taxes so that that property
doesn't go to foreclosure. Whatever they need to do. They have a chance to do that while the
lawsuit is still pending. Then once the lawsuit is done, they get a notice of judgment which allows
them to appeal the judgment within a certain time period again. So they have chance two.
They have several chances along the way in which they can save that property from foreclosure,
and if they fail to do so, I would think it's presumptively, it'll be presumptively
taken that they failed to act within the allotted time. And then if after that time frame passes and
the excess proceeds as we gave in this particular example, and I as the homeowner went forward to
try to claim all of the excess proceeds, I then still have to notify all of the parties
before I'm able to claim the funds. So, again, the mortgage lender has a chance to intervene and say
"Wait a minute, we haven't been paid yet. Give us our money and then you can take the rest." So they
have chance after chance after chance to be able to object, to be able to contest, and to be able
to claim either the property itself or the excess proceeds, or a portion of the excess proceeds. So
that's the short answer to the questions that people are asking regarding Junior Lienholders.
The same goes for every Junior Lienholder that's identified in the tax lawsuit - in the original
tax lawsuit, or any other Junior Lienholders that might be out there that the property owner knows
about. Again, that's procedurally speaking. You could do that and get away with it by claiming
all of the excess proceeds as a former owner as long as you follow all the notice requirements,
and you follow everything to the T. Now, what happens if I did all of that, got all the money,
can the mortgage lender then come back and try to get money from me? Of course they can,
because I still owe them on the debt obligation. But the thing is it's unsecured debt at that
point. There is no more collateral for them to hang it on to, so they can go after me get
a personal judgment against me, I could file for bankruptcy, right? I mean that's just the way it
is in the United States. The bankruptcy laws are there to protect consumers. And sometimes it's
if I don't have the money anymore - maybe I spend $190,000 for medical bills or whatever it is and
I just don't have the money. They can sue me and get a judgment but it's not going to be secured
debt at that point. So that's the downside and disadvantage of the lenders ignoring the tax
lawsuits when they could have acted sooner. So, really, yes they could come after you
after you've taken all of the excess proceeds but in reality, they probably wouldn't come
after you unless it's a ton of money. If it's a ton of money, they could still come after you
but chances are they may not win that lawsuit or if they win, it's going to be a personal judgment
and you can still settle it for a fraction of what you actually owe them. So that's my video for you
for today. Hopefully that's helpful to you and hopefully answers the questions that we get. This
is me summarizing it for educational purposes. The actual reality is that there are many many hoops
and I guess, gymnastics, legal gymnastics that the lawyers have to do to be able to get away
with something like that. So that's my quick answer for you. Hopefully it's been helpful

metadata.title: How To Get Cheap Pre-Foreclosure Motivated Seller Leads From Facebook Ads
metadata.author: Caleb Luketic
metadata.shortDescription:
Get pre-foreclosure leads coming to you asking for help, instead of chasing homeowners with cold calls, cold texts and direct mail. In this video I break down exactly how I'm doing it in my own real estate business with Facebook ads and a free guide for homeowners facing foreclosure, and how my team runs the same campaign for investors all over the country.

Want us to run this in your market? Book a call with me here:
👉 CalebLuketic.com/call

Most motivated seller marketing says the same thing over and over, "we buy houses" and "get your cash offer." This one goes the other way. We give homeowners a free guide built for their state called "What Are Your Options?" that actually helps them understand where they stand, and the ads are simple selfie-style videos that say, if you're facing pre-foreclosure, I've got something free that can help you. There's no pressure in it and none of that closer breath, and people can tell the difference.

When someone grabs the guide, the form asks if they want to sell and how far behind they are, and every lead drops into one of three tracks in GoHighLevel: ready to sell, just gathering info, or already listed on the MLS. The ones who want to sell go straight to your acquisitions team. Everyone else gets helpful text and email follow-up for the long haul, because a lot of these homeowners aren't ready today but will be in six months or a year, and you want to be the one they already trust when that day comes.

When we run this for you, my team builds the guide for your state, launches the ads, and sets up the CRM, pipeline and follow-up automations, so your team only has to talk to the hot leads who actually want to sell. If you already use GoHighLevel we build it right in your account, and if you're on another CRM we can pass the hot leads over to it.

Book a call and we'll break it down for your market: CalebLuketic.com/call
See everything we do for investors and pricing: https://calebluketic.com

CHAPTERS
0:00 Pre-foreclosure leads from Facebook ads
0:25 Why I don't rely on cold calling, texting and direct mail
1:26 The lead magnet idea
2:21 The free "What Are Your Options?" guide
2:59 What the ads look like
3:40 How we turn these leads into deals
4:27 The full lead journey
4:46 The three tracks every seller goes into
5:28 The first 14 days of follow-up
5:58 The texts and emails we send
6:50 Why integrity makes this work
7:28 What it looks like working with me
7:55 The pipeline inside GoHighLevel
8:28 Long-term follow-up for sellers who aren't ready yet
9:23 Book a call

I'm Caleb Luketic, a real estate investor in East Tennessee and the owner of Steel Marketing. We've managed $20M+ in paid ad spend since 2017 and served 1,000+ businesses, real estate investors and home service companies included. Your results will depend on your market, your budget and your follow-up.

Have you tried a lead magnet for pre-foreclosure sellers? Drop a comment and tell me how you're running it, I'm a student of the game too & always trying to learn!

#preforeclosure #realestateinvesting #motivatedsellers #facebookads #Wholesaling #RealEstateLeads

segments.text: Hi everyone, I'm Joseph J. Consul, an
attorney here at ConsulMadison LLP.
Today we're going to talk about a
fascinating but often complex area of
real estate in Philadelphia, sheriff
sales. Oo. and specifically what happens
when you need to file a motion to
complete a sheriff's sale.
Now, if you're familiar, the office of
the sheriff of Philadelphia conducts
monthly auctions of properties that are
in default. Default means people haven't
paid their mortgages or haven't paid
taxes owed to the city.
or there's other judgments against the
property that are pushing these
properties into foreclosure.
These historically have been great
opportunities to acquire property, but
they come with significant
considerations. You'll see properties
sold at mortgage foreclosure auctions
and tax foreclosure auctions, which are
the two main types of auctions.
My number one piece of advice right off
the bat before you even think about
bidding, please do a thorough title
search or at the very least deeply
investigate the property's title
history. Why? because some properties
can be sold subject to prior mortgages
and debts, and you don't want any
surprises after you've made that winning
bid. These days, bidding is conveniently
done online, which makes access easier,
but your due diligence is still
paramount.
While the upside of purchasing a
property at a sheriff sale is clear,
you'll get a property likely at a
significant discount versus purchasing
it on the open market. There's one major
drawback we all too often see at my law
office. That is litigation required
after the sale. You must be prepared for
this. It's common for an interested
third party to file a petition to redeem

segments.text: If your home was sold at a sheriff's sale in New Jersey,
the sale may have brought in more money than the lender was owed.
That extra money does not belong to the lender.
It may belong to you.
In the next few minutes we will explain where that money is,
who gets paid first, and how a claim is made.
I'm Lawrence Friscia, an attorney.
My firm Friscia and Associates, LLC is a New Jersey law firm that handles
surplus funds claims.
This video is general information, not legal advice about your case.
If you would like to speak with us about a surplus funds claim,
the phone number is on the screen and in the description.
Here is how a surplus happens.
The court enters a judgment for what is owed: the loan balance,
interest, and costs.
The sheriff then sells the property to the highest bidder.
If the winning bid is higher than the judgment, the difference is called
surplus funds.
For example, if the judgment is two hundred eighty thousand dollars and
the property sells for three hundred forty thousand,
the surplus is sixty thousand dollars.
If the property sells for less than the judgment, there is no surplus.
Surplus funds are not sent to the former owner automatically.
The money is deposited with the court and held in the Superior Court Trust
Fund until a judge signs an order saying who gets paid.
Nobody receives anything until someone files the right papers and asks.
Who gets the money?
It is paid in order of priority.
Creditors whose liens came after the foreclosed mortgage are first in line.
That can be a second mortgage, a home equity line, or a judgment creditor.
Whatever is left after valid liens belongs to the former owner.
If the owner has died, the claim belongs to the estate,
and the family usually needs authority from the Surrogate before anyone
can apply.
The claim itself is made by motion under Rule four,
sixty-four, dash three.
In plain terms there are five steps.
One, confirm that a surplus exists and how much it is.
Two, find out which liens were on the property, because those creditors
may be paid before you.
Three, file a motion with a certification explaining who you are,
what you are owed, and why your claim comes ahead of anyone else's,
and serve it on every party in the foreclosure case,
including parties who never responded.
Four, the court reviews it and enters an order.
Five, the Trust Fund pays according to that order.
How long do you have?
The rule allows a motion at any time after the sale,
and it sets no fixed deadline.
But waiting carries risk.
Other creditors can file first, records get harder to find,
and money left unclaimed long enough can be turned over to the State.
Most problems come from four places.
The motion was not served on every party.
A lien was missed, and that creditor objects.
The owner has died and no one has authority to act for the estate.
Or the amounts in the proposed order do not match the court's records,
and the order is rejected.
Any one of these can delay payment.
After a sheriff's sale, you may get letters or visits from companies offering
to recover your surplus in exchange for a share of it.
The New Jersey Division of Consumer Affairs has warned that some of these
companies charge as much as seventy-five percent.
The State also points out that many homeowners can file the claim themselves.
So before you sign anything, find out what you are being charged and what
you are getting for it.
When does it make sense to have a lawyer handle it?
When there were other liens on the property.
When the owner has died.
When there was more than one owner.
Or when the amount is large enough that a mistake would be costly.
In those situations, getting the paperwork right the first time can avoid
delays.
If your property was sold at a sheriff's sale in New Jersey and you want
help with a surplus funds claim, call us at Friscia and Associates,
LLC.
Have the property address and the approximate sale date ready.
The number is nine seven three, five hundred, eight zero two four.
The link is in the description.
I'm Lawrence Friscia, with Friscia and Associates, LLC.
This is general information and does not create an attorney-client relationship.
Thank you for watching.
